papers.title: Optimal Trading Filters and the Value of Predictive Signals
papers.abstract: The value of a forecast depends on its accuracy, but also on its actionability. In trading, an investor must translate return forecasts into positions while accounting for trading costs and the lingering impact of earlier trades. We solve the stationary quadratic trading problem with transient price impact using tools from prediction theory: Wiener-Hopf factorization gives the optimal policy as the composition of a conditional forecast and an explicit causal linear filter. We recover the Gârleanu-Pedersen aim-portfolio under exponential resilience and derive fractional trading filters under power-law impact decay, requiring memory beyond finite-dimensional LQR control. At fixed positive risk penalty, signals of equal instantaneous predictive strength have equal frictionless Markowitz value. With trading costs, net attainable value is determined by the mean square of the friction-weighted conditional forecast. Under power-law impact with exposure bleeding, we find an intermediate optimal mean-reversion rate for Ornstein-Uhlenbeck signals.

papers.title: Do Econophysics-Inspired Inputs Improve Neural Covariance Forecasting? A Leakage-Free Walk-Forward Study of Intraday DJIA Data
papers.abstract: Tools from econophysics, including Random Matrix Theory (RMT), Tsallis q-Gaussian tails, Hawkes self-excitation and diffusion-inspired regularization, are often proposed as ingredients for financial risk models, but their incremental value over strong contemporary benchmarks remains unclear. We introduce a Physics-Inspired Neural Covariance (PINC) framework for one-day-ahead covariance forecasting using 1-minute data from the 29 Dow Jones Industrial Average constituents over 545 trading days. The model incorporates RMT-cleaned correlations, Tsallis tail indices and Hawkes intensities as inputs and optionally includes a Fokker-Planck-inspired regularization term selected strictly on validation data. Evaluation is performed through a nested walk-forward design with 11 folds, 231 out-of-sample trading days and multiple random seeds, with explicit leakage controls and reproducibility tests. Neural models outperform static covariance estimators such as sample, Ledoit-Wolf, RMT and EVT-based estimators, but show no statistically significant improvement over HAR-RV or LSTM benchmarks. Validation consistently rejects the physics-inspired regularizer, and ablation studies find no measurable contribution from the RMT, Tsallis or Hawkes features. Portfolio experiments show no statistically significant Sharpe ratio improvement after transaction costs. These results suggest that, for this dataset and forecasting horizon, econophysics-inspired components do not provide measurable benefits beyond strong financial forecasting benchmarks.
papers.comment: 8 pages, 7 figures, 4 tables. Empirical study on covariance forecasting, econophysics-inspired machine learning, portfolio optimization, and risk forecasting. Submitted to Results in Physics

papers.title: Report2Alpha-Bench: Evaluating LLM Agents on End-to-End Quantitative Research
papers.abstract: We evaluate whether LLM agents can independently carry out a several-hour quantitative research project: read a brokerage research report, make a plan, and over 7 rounds of iteration propose hypotheses, write factor code and improve it from backtest feedback, seeing only 2022-2023 market data. Like Terminal-Bench-Science, the task evaluates overall research ability; unlike it, there is no directly checkable unique answer: the model must repeatedly propose hypotheses on very noisy data, revise its understanding from experiments, disentangle multiple factors and design ablations without overfitting in-sample, much like complex real-world decisions with many interacting factors. After the research, a fixed rule using only 2022-2023 results selects a low-correlated factor pool from all candidates the model produced, and scores it on unseen 2024-2025 data after removing common style returns such as size and momentum; the same rule on round-0 candidates alone gives a report baseline that "implements the report without iterating". We run gpt-6.1-sol (reasoning effort xhigh), gpt-6.1-terra (xhigh), muse-spark-1.3 (xhigh) and deepseek-v4.1-flash (max) once on each of 7 reports. Of the 28 runs, 19 factor pools pass the usability threshold; the average score is 48.4 (0-100 scale), against 25.4 for the report baseline and 35.9 for the models' own picks. From similar report baselines (17.0-31.0), the models separate after iteration to 74.7 (gpt-6.1-sol), 56.6 (gpt-6.1-terra), 35.8 (deepseek-v4.1-flash) and 26.2 (muse-spark-1.3); their candidates look equally good in training and diverge only in testing, with the leaders proposing more diverse ideas per round and ending with more effective factors in the pool. Evaluating research agents thus requires scoring on frozen future data after removing styles, and measuring "what the research produced" separately from "what was finally picked".

papers.title: Semi-Static Variance-Optimal Hedging of Covariance Risk in Multi-Asset Derivatives
papers.abstract: We develop a semi-static framework for the variance-optimal hedging of multi-asset derivatives exposed to correlation and covariance risk. The approach combines continuous-time dynamic trading in the underlying assets with a static portfolio of auxiliary contingent claims. Using a multivariate Galtchouk--Kunita--Watanabe decomposition, we show that the resulting global mean-variance problem decouples naturally into an inner continuous-time projection onto the space spanned by the underlying assets and an outer finite-dimensional quadratic optimization over the static hedging instruments. To systematically select suitable auxiliary claims, we leverage multidimensional functional spanning theory, establishing that otherwise unhedgeable cross-gamma exposures can be structurally mitigated through static strips of vanilla, product, and spread options. As a central application, we derive explicit semi-static replication formulas for covariance swaps and geometric dispersion trades. Our framework accommodates a broad class of asset dynamics, including quadratic and stochastic Volterra covariance models, as well as affine stochastic covariance models with jumps, yielding tractable semi-closed-form solutions via Fourier transform techniques. Extensive numerical experiments demonstrate that incorporating optimally weighted static strips of cross-asset instruments substantially reduces the mean-squared hedging error relative to purely dynamic benchmark strategies across various model classes.

papers.title: Do Better Volatility Forecasts Lead to Better Portfolios? Evidence from Graph Neural Networks
papers.abstract: This paper tests whether graph neural networks improve realized volatility forecasts and whether those forecasts improve portfolio performance. Using weekly realized volatility for 465 S&P 500 equities from 2015-2025, Heterogeneous Autoregressive and Long Short-Term Memory baselines are compared against GraphSAGE models built on rolling correlation, sector, and Granger-causal graphs, with and without macro regime features. The empirical finding is that the model with the lowest forecast MSE, the model with the highest cross-sectional ranking accuracy, and the model with the highest portfolio Sharpe ratio are three different models. Forecast accuracy, ranking quality, and portfolio performance are related but not interchangeable objectives. Graph volatility models add value only when the portfolio rule can exploit the cross-sectional structure they encode.

papers.title: Forecasting Equity Correlations with Hybrid Transformer Graph Neural Network
papers.abstract: This paper studies forward-looking stock-stock correlation forecasting for S\&P 500 constituents and evaluates whether learned correlation forecasts can improve graph-based clustering used in basket trading strategies. We cast 10-day ahead correlation prediction in Fisher-z space and train a Temporal-Heterogeneous Graph Neural Network (THGNN) to predict residual deviations from a rolling historical baseline. The architecture combines a Transformer-based temporal encoder, which captures non-stationary, complex, temporal dependencies, with an edge-aware graph attention network that propagates cross-asset information over the equity network. Inputs span daily returns, technicals, sector structure, previous correlations, and macro signals, enabling regime-aware forecasts and attention-based feature and neighbor importance to provide interpretability. Out-of-sample results from 2019-2024 show that the proposed model meaningfully reduces correlation forecasting error relative to rolling-window estimates. When integrated into a graph-based clustering framework, forward-looking correlations produce adaptable and economically meaningfully baskets, particularly during periods of market stress. These findings suggest that improvements in correlation forecasts translate into meaningful gains during portfolio construction tasks.

papers.title: Mitigating Return Drag and Regime Whipsaws in Sector Rotation: An Asymmetric Downside-Aware Nested Clustered Optimization Framework
papers.abstract: Hierarchical clustering and Nested Clustered Optimization (NCO) mitigate the mathematical ill-conditioning of classical Markowitz covariance matrices. However, two structural vulnerabilities persist in equity markets: (1) symmetric variance penalizes upside and downside return dispersion identically, inducing acute return drag against soaring momentum sectors; and (2) unconstrained Hidden Markov Models (HMM) exhibit hyper-active regime switching (whipsaw instability), incurring excessive turnover and transaction drag. We propose Asymmetric Downside-Risk Nested Clustered Optimization with Sticky Regime Dynamics (Asym-Sticky-NCO) for tactical sector rotation across all 11 S&P 500 GICS sectors. The framework substitutes symmetric covariance with the Bawa-Lindenberg downside semi-covariance matrix across both hierarchical tree clustering and two-stage allocation. Furthermore, we introduce a Sticky Gaussian HMM incorporating a diagonal self-transition persistence prior (\k{appa}) and confidence-adaptive boundaries (δ) to enforce macroeconomic persistence. Strictly non-anticipative walk-forward backtesting across 65 out-of-sample months (August 2020 to December 2025) demonstrates that the architecture elevates CAGR from 10.65% (Plain NCO) to 13.41% (+276 bps/year), delivers a 97.74% total return versus 72.99%, suppresses maximum drawdown to 14.22% (versus 23.93% for the S&P 500), and achieves a Calmar ratio of 0.94 (+38.2% over S&P 500; +84.3% over Baseline Regime-NCO). Crucially, sticky dynamics cut regime whipsaws by 75.0% (from 16 to 4 switches) and reduce monthly turnover from 60.78% to 30.48%, addressing core limitations of machine learning asset allocation.
papers.comment: 7 pages, 6 figures, 4 tables. Code available at: https://github.com/obo-cloud/sp500-asymmetric-nco

papers.title: Uniform-Loss Automated Market Making for Prediction Markets
papers.abstract: Automated market makers (AMMs) for prediction markets descend from market scoring rules, where a mechanism operator subsidizes a market to aggregate beliefs about uncertain events. The existing literature has focused on bounding the total worst-case loss to the subsidizer, but has not addressed how that loss is distributed across price states or over time. We use the framework of loss-versus-rebalancing (LVR) to study this distribution and introduce \textit{uniform AMMs}, defined by the property that instantaneous LVR is proportional to pool value and independent of the current token price. In a static setting, we show that for a broad class of \textit{win-martingales} -- processes that converge to 0 or 1 at a fixed resolution time -- there exists a pricing function that achieves uniform LVR under that process, and conversely, that any sufficiently regular pricing function induces a win-martingale under which it is uniform. We then extend the framework to dynamic liquidity management, showing that liquidity levels can be adjusted over time to implement a prescribed target expected cumulative loss schedule. This theory is illustrated with canonical examples of win-martingales and pricing functions. Our results can inform AMM designers and liquidity providers on how the inevitable cost of subsidizing price discovery can be shaped and controlled across both price and time.

papers.title: On Reference-Regulated Multiperiod Mean-Variance Portfolio Optimization in High Dimensions
papers.abstract: The multiperiod mean-variance (MV) portfolio optimization serves as a vital expansion of Markowitz's static MV portfolio selection framework. Just like its static counterpart, the multiperiod MV portfolio remains susceptible to estimation errors. We propose a reference-regulated multiperiod mean-variance (RRMV) framework that penalizes deviations from a reference policy. Therefore, this new optimization successfully combines the advantages of dynamic strategies and reference portfolios. A key contribution of this paper is the characterization of the out-of-sample Sharpe ratio under high-dimensional asymptotics with estimation errors in both the mean vector and the covariance matrix. We show how the reference penalty and the investment horizon jointly affect the optimized portfolio performance, and how regularization operates differently from the single-period portfolio optimization. Extensive simulation and real data studies demonstrate that the proposed framework improves the stability and out-of-sample Sharpe ratios of multiperiod policies significantly.

summary.method: 提出參考規範多期均值-變異數（RRMV）最佳化框架並結合高維度漸近分析，透過模擬與真實資料進行實證研究。
summary.findings: 透過模擬與真實資料研究證明，該框架顯著提升多期策略的穩定性與樣本外 Sharpe，但論文未報告具體的績效數字。
summary.implication: 可用於多期資產配置以降低估計誤差的衝擊，前提是須妥善設定參考策略與懲罰參數。
summary.caveats: 依賴高維度漸近理論，懲罰參數與投資期限的設定對實際表現影響重大。

papers.title: When the Rules Change: Adaptive Signal Extraction via Kalman Filtering and Markov-Switching Regimes
papers.abstract: Most empirical microstructure research assumes that order flow--return parameters are constant, yet these relationships shift substantially across market regimes. Combining adaptive Kalman filtering, Markov-switching regime identification, and asymmetric response estimation, we characterize regime-dependent investor behavior in the Korean stock market during 2020--2024 using daily transaction data disaggregated by investor type. Three principal findings emerge: foreign investor predictive power increases several-fold during crisis periods relative to bull markets; individual investors chase momentum asymmetrically, reacting far more strongly to positive than to negative shocks; and independent information-theoretic validation corroborates both patterns. Rigorous out-of-sample testing reveals that these in-sample regularities do not generalize reliably, underscoring the need for proper validation methodology in microstructure research.
papers.relevance_reason: 結合卡爾曼濾波與體制轉換分析投資人行為，發現樣本外檢驗無法泛化。

summary.title_zh: 當規則改變時：透過卡爾曼濾波與馬可夫體制轉換進行適應性信號萃取
summary.verdict: 結合卡爾曼濾波與馬可夫體制轉換分析韓國市場，發現外資預測力在危機時大增，但樣本外泛化能力不足。
summary.problem: 多數實證市場微結構研究假設訂單流與報酬參數為常數，忽略了這些關係會在不同市場體制間大幅變動。
summary.method: 使用自我調整卡爾曼濾波、馬可夫體制轉換識別與非對稱反應估計，分析韓國股市 2020 年至 2024 年依投資人類別拆分的日頻交易資料。
summary.findings: 外資的預測能力在危機期間較多頭市場增加數倍；散戶會非對稱地追逐動能，對正面衝擊的反應遠大於負面衝擊。論文未報告具體績效數字。
summary.implication: 雖然能捕捉到體制轉換下的投資人行為差異，但由於嚴格的樣本外測試顯示規律無法可靠泛化，實際交易前需重新設計驗證方法。
summary.caveats: 實證發現的樣本內規律無法可靠地進行樣本外泛化。
